content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.92, after using 32 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, `L1-S1-M1` and `L3-S2-M4`. Then I used the free `compare` command to pick test tasks where the two hypotheses predict opposite results:

| Test task | Rules new to the learner | Best similarity to a trained task | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| `L3-S1-M1` | 0 | 0.00 | 46.8 (n=12, median 43) |
| `L2-S3-M2` | 3 | 0.56 | 25.1 (n=12, median 17) |
| `L1-S1-M2` | 1 | 0.75 | 12.7 (n=6) |

**Evidence:** The task built only from trained rules was the hardest to learn. The task with three new rules was learned about twice as fast. Learning cost went down as similarity to the trained mappings went up, which is what the holistic hypothesis predicts. The part-based hypothesis predicts the reverse: `L3-S1-M1` should have been the easiest.

The tests were noisy; single results for the same task ranged from 1 to 70. The main gap (about 47 vs 25 over 12 runs each) is roughly 2–2.5 standard errors on its own. I put confidence at 0.92 because the three tasks also fall in the order similarity predicts and the medians differ more than the means.
